name: Yara Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of three reporters on a weekly paper that covers a market town and about twenty villages around it. Monday is the parish council and the magistrates' list, Tuesday is phoning round churches, schools and the farming club, and Wednesday night we put the paper to bed. I write everything in a notebook first and type it up after, and I've never used one of those AI writing things. I don't see the point when I can write it myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that people stop me in the butcher's to tell me about their grandson's football or the hedge that's blocking the lane. I grew up here, I sing in the church choir on Sundays, and the paper is how the town talks to itself. What wears me down is the owners, a group in the city that's bought up fifteen weeklies and keeps cutting the page count. I live with my fiancé Joel, who's a farm machinery mechanic, and we've got roughly three months of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that'd suit me fine, honestly. Hype is what I always thought it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely, probably at the choir tea. People round here are suspicious of anything from the big tech firms anyway, so I'd be saying what they already think. I wouldn't post about it online, because I don't really do that outside the paper's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never my biggest worry. My worry is the owners closing us or merging us with the paper in the next town, which they've done to two other weeklies in the group already. That doesn't change if AI turns out to be hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep my head down. I'd try to put another fifty a month aside, because Joel and I are saving for the wedding next autumn and I'd like a bit more cover in case the paper goes. I'd also ask the editor whether I could take on the farming pages properly, because that's the section readers still pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the machines, about the paper's owners, which is the same worry I go to bed with now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owners merged two other weeklies. What happened to the reporters there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of them, Hannah, who I trained with, got moved to a hub office forty minutes away and writes for three towns she's never lived in. The other two took redundancy. Hannah says she spends half her day rewriting press releases now instead of going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the paper were merged, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try not to go to the hub. I'd ask around at the auction mart and the agricultural college about press work, or my dad might take me on at his feed and seed shop for a bit. I wouldn't want to leave town, because Joel's work is here and so is my church.

say: She'd say she always thought the AI talk was **hype**.
People round here already **distrust** big tech firms, so she'd be echoing them.
think: Her real worry is the **owners** closing or merging the paper.
AI being hype doesn't change the **page cuts** she already lives with.
do: Keep working as she is and **keep her head down**.
Save an extra **fifty a month** towards the wedding and a cushion.
Ask to take on the **farming pages**, the section readers still pay for.
feel: **Uneasy** about the owners, the same worry she already goes to bed with.
S0.quote: My worry is the owners closing us or merging us with the paper in the next town, which they've done to two other weeklies in the group already.
fieldNote: Her biggest fear is the **owning group**, not technology.
She's deeply rooted: **choir, church, Joel's work** and her dad's shop all tie her to town.
She has a quiet **fallback** in her father's feed and seed shop.
Hannah's move to a **hub office** is her picture of what going wrong looks like.

steps.text: Keep writing the council, courts and community pages as now
Put an extra fifty a month towards the wedding and savings
Ask the editor to give her the farming pages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one sounds more like what the owners are hoping for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a computer can't sit at the back of a parish council meeting and notice who didn't turn up. I'd say it at work and at the choir and to anyone who asked. I'd also say people should buy the paper if they want it to survive, because nothing's free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the owners would use it as an excuse to cut us from three reporters to one, with software filling the pages from press releases. I'm the youngest and the newest, so I'd be the one most likely to go, even though I know the town best. That's what really frightens me in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start building up the farming pages now, because the auction reports and the show results are things nobody else does properly. I'd stop the extra fifty for the wedding and put it straight into savings instead, and we'd do the reception in the church hall rather than the hotel. If they cut a post, I'd go and talk to the agricultural college about their press and communications job before the hub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. Would you try them now, to stay on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so, honestly. Maybe if the editor made me, for typing up the court list. But I'd feel like I was training my own replacement, and I'm stubborn about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your post went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners first, because they look at a spreadsheet and not at the town. A little bit the readers too, if I'm honest, the ones who read us free on their phones and then complain when there's no reporter at the flower show. I wouldn't blame the government, because it's not their job to keep a newspaper going.

say: A computer can't sit at a **parish council** meeting and notice who's missing.
People should **buy the paper** if they want it to survive.
think: The owners would cut **three reporters to one** and fill pages from press releases.
As the **youngest and newest**, she'd likely be the one to go.
do: Build up the **farming pages** with auction reports and show results.
Move wedding savings into a cushion and hold the reception in the **church hall**.
Approach the **agricultural college** about its press job if a post is cut.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a letter she knows is coming.
S1.quote: A computer can't sit at the back of a parish council meeting and notice who didn't turn up.
fieldNote: She refuses AI tools because it feels like **training her replacement**.
She blames the **owners** first and free-reading readers second, not the government.
She expects to be **first out** despite knowing the town best.
The **wedding** is where she'd cut back first.

steps.text: Build up the farming pages with auction reports and show results
Redirect the extra fifty a month from wedding fund to savings
Hold the wedding reception in the church hall instead of the hotel
Ask the agricultural college about its press job if her post goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before our wedding has even been paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we've got to look after our own, our families and our churches, because the big firms won't. I'd probably say it in an editorial if they still let me write one. I'd also say I don't believe a machine will ever really know this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the paper would be gone, or turned into a machine feed with our name on it, by 2028. Nearly everything I do is thinking and writing, and the hands-on bits, driving to the show ground and standing in the rain, aren't really what anyone pays for. Robots coming three years later wouldn't save my job, but it might mean Joel's work fixing tractors lasts a bit longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad straight away about working at the feed and seed shop, at first part-time on Saturdays so I learn the stock. We'd cut right back: no holiday next year, sell my car and share Joel's van. I'd keep the reporting going as long as they paid me, but I'd stop thinking of it as my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And a bit ashamed, because I'd always thought I'd be the one people in town came to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Joel's work might last longer than yours. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. My mum stayed home and my dad's always been the main wage, so I don't mind if Joel carries us for a while. What I'd mind is being useless, not being second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the readers in your last edition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd thank them and tell them to keep going to the parish meetings themselves, because nobody else will be there to write it down. I'd probably cry writing it. I'd put a list of who to phone at the council in the back.

say: We've got to **look after our own**, because the big firms won't.
A machine will never really **know this town**.
think: The paper is **gone** or turned into a **feed** by 2028.
Robots coming later might keep **Joel's tractor work** going longer than her job.
do: Start **Saturday shifts** at her dad's feed and seed shop to learn the stock.
Cut back hard: **no holiday**, sell her car, share Joel's van.
Keep reporting while paid, but stop treating it as her **career**.
feel: **Frightened**, and **ashamed** at no longer being who the town comes to.
S2.quote: Robots coming three years later wouldn't save my job, but it might mean Joel's work fixing tractors lasts a bit longer than mine.
fieldNote: She expects the paper to be **gone within two years** and says so flatly.
Her plan runs through **family**: her dad's shop and Joel's wage.
She's comfortable being **second earner**, but fears being useless.
Her last-edition answer shows real **civic duty** under the gloom.

steps.text: Work Saturday shifts at her dad's feed and seed shop
Sell her car and share Joel's van
Lean on Joel's wage while she moves to the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but I'd add that young people should be learning a trade, not just going to university. I'd say it at the young farmers and on the paper's letters page. I'd be a bit of a hypocrite saying it, with my journalism degree, and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years buys me maybe three or four years of the paper, but the end's the same. I'd be watching every quarter for the owners' announcement. And I don't think I'd get any new reporting job, because every other paper would be going the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over the shop's books and the ordering properly, over the first couple of years, because my dad wants to retire at some point anyway. I'd do an evening bookkeeping course at the college so I know what I'm doing. We'd still get married next autumn, but small, and we'd hold off on a house for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, just more slowly. Like the same bad news, but by post instead of by phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take over the shop's ordering. Isn't that thinking work too, the kind AI does first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I hadn't thought of that. Dad does the ordering from a paper catalogue and the reps visit in person, so maybe it lasts a bit. But I suppose the ordering could be done by a computer, and what's left is me behind the counter talking to farmers about their feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of being a reporter would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The court list. Not the drama, but sitting there seeing how the town is really doing, who's in trouble, who's drinking too much. You know a place differently after a year of the magistrates' court.

say: Young people should be **learning a trade**, not just going to university.
She'd say it at the **young farmers** and on the letters page.
think: Five years buys **three or four** more years of the paper, with the same end.
She doubts she'd find **any reporting job** elsewhere.
do: Take over the **books and ordering** at her dad's shop over two years.
Do an evening **bookkeeping course** at the college.
Marry next autumn but **small**, and hold off on buying a house.
feel: **Frightened**, just more slowly, like bad news arriving by post.
S3.quote: Five years buys me maybe three or four years of the paper, but the end's the same.
fieldNote: She admits being a **hypocrite** about trades, with her own journalism degree.
She hadn't seen that **shop ordering** is also thinking work AI takes first.
What she'd miss is the **court list**, which is how she reads the town.
Extra time changes her **pace**, not her expectation of losing the job.

steps.text: Take over the books and ordering at her dad's feed and seed shop
Do an evening bookkeeping course at the agricultural college
Hold a small wedding and delay buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Well, I'd be thirty-seven and probably have children by then, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time for the town to decide what it wants to keep. Maybe a paper owned by the town itself, like the cricket club is. I'd say it at a town meeting if anyone organised one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd still lose the job, just later. But ten years is enough for Joel and me to have a family and get a house before it hits. And it's enough for me to learn the shop properly instead of being thrown into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for now and help at the shop on Saturdays. We'd marry next autumn, the proper wedding, and try for a baby in a couple of years. I'd put a bit away each month for a few years, maybe a hundred, so when the change comes I've got something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe in this one. It's the first one where I can picture a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a paper owned by the town. Would you be part of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to be, but I'd want someone else to do the money side, because I don't trust myself with it. If the vicar and the mart owner and a few farmers chipped in, I'd write it for a small wage. I don't know if anyone would pay, though, and I'd say that honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you stay a reporter all the way to the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the town paper happened. Otherwise no, I think I'm realistic. In ten years I'd rather be the woman behind the counter who still knows everybody's news than a reporter at a hub forty minutes away.

say: Ten years is time for the town to decide what it wants to **keep**.
A **town-owned paper**, like the cricket club, could be an answer.
think: She'd still **lose the job**, just later.
Ten years lets her and Joel have a **family and a house** first.
do: Keep reporting and help at the **shop on Saturdays**.
Have the **proper wedding** next autumn and try for a baby in two years.
Save about **a hundred a month** as a fallback.
feel: Uneasy, but she can **breathe**; it's the first version with a **normal life**.
S4.quote: In ten years I'd rather be the woman behind the counter who still knows everybody's news than a reporter at a hub forty minutes away.
fieldNote: Even with a decade, she still **expects to lose** the reporting job.
The town-owned paper is a hope she **doubts** anyone would fund.
The extra time protects her **family plans** above all.
She'd rather stay **local** in a different job than follow work to a hub.

steps.text: Keep reporting for the weekly paper for now
Marry next autumn and try for a baby in two years
Save about a hundred a month as a fallback
Help at her dad's shop on Saturdays to learn it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I do is writing and asking questions, and two years isn't time to do anything except run to my dad's shop. What would help is the paper's owners selling it to the town for a fair price instead of shutting it, and the college running short practical courses for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church, and it matters. If the paper goes, the church noticeboard and the Sunday notices are how half the old people in town will hear anything. I'd probably end up writing the parish newsletter for nothing, and I'd be glad to.

headlineQuote: If the paper goes, the church noticeboard and the Sunday notices are how half the old people in town will hear anything.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old** reporter on a market-town weekly, covering councils, courts, churches and farming.
She writes in a **notebook**, has never used AI, and sees using it as training her replacement.
She's engaged to Joel, a **farm machinery mechanic**, with about three months saved and a wedding next autumn.
Her standing fear is the **owning group** merging the paper; AI makes her the likely first cut.
In every faster scenario she falls back on **family**: her dad's feed and seed shop and Joel's wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves her nothing but running to her dad's shop.
whatWouldHelp: The owners selling the paper to the **town** for a fair price.
Short **practical courses** at the local college.
